steps.title: Saying hello
steps.body: German greetings change with the time of day and with how well you know someone. Hallo works almost anywhere with people your age. Guten Tag is the safe, neutral choice with strangers.
points: Guten Morgen until about 10 or 11 am
Gute Nacht only when someone is going to bed

steps.note: The g in Tag sounds like k at the end of the word.

steps.prompt: It is 8 pm and you walk into a restaurant. What do you say?
steps.explain: Gute Nacht is only used when someone is going to sleep.

steps.title: sein and heißen
steps.body: Two verbs get you through any introduction. sein means to be, heißen means to be called. Use du with friends, family and children, and Sie with everyone else.

steps.prompt: You meet your new manager. Which question fits?
steps.explain: Sie is the polite form for people you don't know well, especially at work.
ich always takes bin.

steps.title: kommen aus, wohnen in
steps.body: Say where you are from with kommen aus and where you live with wohnen in. Most countries take no article, but a few do, and then aus changes the article.

steps.explain: Origin is always aus.
aus is followed by the dative, so die Schweiz becomes der Schweiz.

steps.de: Ich komme aus Indien und wohne in München.
steps.en: I'm from India and live in Munich.

steps.de: Ich komme aus Amerika und wohne in Hamburg.
steps.en: I'm from America and live in Hamburg.

steps.title: The first numbers
steps.body: These twelve are the building blocks for everything else. Watch the sounds: z in zwei and zehn is ts, ü in fünf needs rounded lips, and ch in acht is the throaty ach sound.

steps.prompt: How is z pronounced in zehn?

steps.title: Units before tens
steps.body: From 21 on, German says the unit first: einundzwanzig is literally one-and-twenty. The tens mostly end in -zig, with dreißig (30) as the exception.

steps.explain: sieben (7) und vierzig (40) gives 47.

steps.de: Meine Nummer ist null, eins, sieben, sechs.
steps.en: My number is zero, one, seven, six.

steps.title: haben, and age with sein
steps.body: haben means to have. Age, though, uses sein, like English: Ich bin 25 Jahre alt.

steps.de: Meine Tochter ist sieben Jahre alt.
steps.en: My daughter is seven years old.

steps.title: Every noun has a gender
steps.body: German nouns are masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The gender is often not logical, so always learn a noun together with its article. In this app der is blue, die is red and das is green.
points: Words ending in -chen and -lein are das
Male people are usually der, female people die

steps.explain: Words ending in -ung are always die.
-chen always makes a word das, even when it means a girl.

steps.de: der Vater, die Mutter, das Kind
steps.en: the father, the mother, the child

steps.title: mein and dein
steps.body: mein (my) and dein (your) take an -e before feminine and plural nouns.

steps.explain: das Kind is neuter, so no -e.
Plural takes meine.

steps.de: Mein Vater heißt Peter und meine Mutter heißt Julia.
steps.en: My father is called Peter and my mother is called Julia.

steps.title: Adjectives after sein
steps.body: After sein an adjective needs no ending: Er ist groß. Sie ist nett. Endings only appear when the adjective comes before the noun, which you will meet later.

steps.de: Mein Großvater ist alt, aber fit.
steps.en: My grandfather is old but fit.

steps.prompt: The plural of die Mutter is...
steps.explain: Many plurals add an umlaut. Muttern exists, but it means screw nuts.

steps.de: Meine Familie ist klein, aber sehr glücklich.
steps.en: My family is small but very happy.

steps.de: Ich habe einen Bruder. Er heißt Jonas und er ist sehr groß.
steps.en: I have a brother. His name is Jonas and he is very tall.

steps.title: Ordering with möchten
steps.body: möchten (would like) is the polite way to order. Ich hätte gern... is just as common and means the same.

steps.en: What would you like to drink?

steps.prompt: The waiter asks: Was möchten Sie? You answer:

steps.en: I would like a tea, please.

steps.de: Zwei Kaffee und ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
steps.en: Two coffees and a piece of cake, please.

steps.de: Ich möchte einen Kaffee mit Milch, bitte.
steps.en: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

steps.title: The accusative, first look
steps.body: The thing you want, buy or eat is the object of the sentence. In that position only masculine words change: der becomes den and ein becomes einen. Feminine and neuter stay the same.

steps.explain: der Apfel is masculine, so ein becomes einen.
das Brot is neuter, no change.

steps.de: Ich nehme einen Tee und ein Ei.
steps.en: I'll have a tea and an egg.

steps.de: Ich esse einen Apfel und ein Ei.
steps.en: I'm eating an apple and an egg.

steps.title: kein and gern
steps.body: kein means no or not any, and takes the same endings as ein. Put gern after the verb to say you like doing something.

steps.explain: die Zeit is feminine, so keine.
das Bier is neuter.

steps.de: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, aber ich trinke gern Tee.
steps.en: I don't drink coffee, but I like drinking tea.

steps.de: Ich esse gern Brot mit Käse.
steps.en: I like eating bread with cheese.

steps.title: Regular Verbs
steps.body: In German, verbs change their endings to match the person speaking. To conjugate a regular verb, take the infinitive (like *machen*) and remove the *-en* to find the stem (*mach-*). Then, add the correct ending: *-e* for "I", *-st* for "you", and *-t* for "he/she/it". Unlike English, which mostly only changes for the third person, German uses different endings for almost every subject.

steps.explain: For the first person singular 'ich', we add the ending '-e'.
For the second person singular 'du', we add the ending '-st'.
For the third person singular 'er', we add the ending '-t'.

steps.title: The Verb is Second
steps.body: In German, the conjugated verb must always be the second element in a standard statement. In English, we often say "Today I drink," but in German, the verb must stay in that second slot. If you start a sentence with a time expression, the subject must move to the third position to keep the verb in place.

steps.de: Um acht Uhr trinke ich Kaffee.
steps.en: At eight o'clock I drink coffee.

steps.explain: The verb must be the second element in the sentence.
The time expression is the first element, so the verb must come next.
In a standard sentence starting with the subject, the verb is the second element.

steps.en: At eight o'clock I eat breakfast.

steps.title: Time Expressions
steps.body: To express time in German, you must choose the correct preposition based on what you are describing. For specific clock times, use **um** (at). For parts of the day, use **am** (in the). For frequency, use **jeden** (every). This is more specific than English, which often uses 'at' or 'in' more broadly.

steps.explain: We use 'um' for specific clock times.

steps.prompt: How do you say 'in the morning'?
steps.explain: 'Am' is used for parts of the day.
'Jeden' is the correct word for 'every'.

steps.title: The phrase 'es gibt'
steps.body: In English, we change between 'there is' and 'there are.' In German, we always use 'es gibt' for both singular and plural. It is a fixed expression that means 'there is' or 'there are.'

steps.note: Use 'keine' to say there is 'no' or 'not a' thing.

steps.explain: 'Es gibt' is the fixed phrase for 'there is' or 'there are.'
'Lampe' is feminine, so we use 'eine'.

steps.title: Plural Forms
steps.body: In English, you usually just add "-s" to make a word plural. In German, nouns change in different ways: some add "-e", some add "-en", and some change their vowel. Most importantly, you cannot use "a" or "an" (ein/eine) when you are talking about more than one thing.

steps.explain: The plural of "Tisch" is formed by adding "-e".
"Buch" changes its vowel to "ü" and adds "-er" in the plural.
The plural of "Stuhl" is "Stühle".

steps.title: Where is it?
steps.body: To ask about the location of an object, use "Wo ist...?" for one item and "Wo sind...?" for multiple items. This follows the same logic as the English "Where is...?" and "Where are...?" patterns. The key is to match the verb to whether the object you are looking for is singular or plural.

steps.explain: "Das Buch" is singular, so we use "ist."
"Die Bücher" is plural, so we use "sind."
"Die Lampen" is plural, so we use "sind."

title: Polite Directions: The Imperative with Sie

steps.title: The Polite Imperative (Sie)
steps.body: When giving directions to strangers, German uses the formal 'Sie' form to be polite. Unlike English, where we often just say 'Go left,' German requires you to use the verb followed by 'Sie.' It is very simple: use the standard verb form and add 'Sie' immediately after it. This turns a statement into a polite command.

steps.explain: To give a polite command, use the verb followed by 'Sie'.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct way to say 'Go straight'?
steps.explain: A polite command requires both the verb and the word 'Sie'.

steps.prompt: How do you say 'Take the bus' politely?
steps.explain: Use the verb followed by 'Sie' and include the necessary article 'den'.

steps.title: Using können (can/to be able to)
steps.body: The verb *können* means 'can' or 'to be able to.' When you use *können* in a sentence, the second verb (the action) must move to the very end of the sentence in its infinitive form. In English, we say 'I can go,' but in German, the action verb stays at the end. This structure is essential for asking questions and making statements about ability.

steps.de: Ich kann mit dem Bus fahren.

steps.prompt: How do you ask 'Can you help me?' (polite)?
steps.explain: In a question, the conjugated verb (können) comes first, followed by the subject (Sie).

steps.prompt: Choose the correct form: 'Ich ___ mit dem Bus fahren.'
steps.explain: The first-person singular form of können is 'ich kann'.

steps.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'Wir können zu Fuß ___.'
steps.explain: When using a modal verb like können, the second verb must be in its infinitive form (ending in -en) at the end of the sentence.

steps.de: Ich kann mit dem Bus fahren.

title: Getting Around: By Bus or On Foot

steps.title: How to travel
steps.body: To describe how you travel, use 'mit' plus the vehicle. In German, 'mit' always triggers the dative case, so 'der Bus' becomes 'mit dem Bus.' For walking, use the fixed expression 'zu Fuß.' Unlike English, which uses 'by,' German uses 'with' (mit).

steps.en: Use 'fahren' for vehicles and 'gehen' for walking.

steps.explain: 'Bus' is masculine, and 'mit' requires the dative case, changing 'der' to 'dem'.
'Zu Fuß' is a fixed idiomatic expression in German.

steps.prompt: Complete the sentence: 'Ich fahre ___.' (I go by train.)
steps.explain: 'Zug' is masculine, so 'mit' changes 'der' to 'dem'.

steps.title: Separable Verbs (Trennbare Verben)
steps.body: In German, some verbs have a prefix that 'splits off' and moves to the end of the sentence. While English uses phrasal verbs like 'to turn off,' German keeps the main verb in the second position and pushes the prefix to the very last spot. This separation is a key part of many common German verbs.

steps.note: The prefix 'an' always moves to the very end of the clause.

steps.prompt: How do you say 'I watch TV'?
steps.explain: The prefix 'fern-' must move to the end of the sentence.
The prefix 'ein-' must move to the end of the sentence.

steps.title: Using gern and lieber
steps.body: In English, we often use the verb 'to like' (e.g., I like to swim). In German, you do not use a separate verb for 'like' when describing an action. Instead, you use the adverb *gern* placed directly after the verb. To say you prefer one activity over another, use *lieber* instead of *gern*.

steps.prompt: How do you say 'I like to sing'?
steps.explain: In German, you express liking an activity by adding 'gern' after the verb.

steps.prompt: How do you say 'I prefer to play'?
steps.explain: 'Lieber' is used to express a preference for one thing over another.
'Lieber' indicates a preference, whereas 'gern' would mean you simply like it.

steps.title: Negation: nicht vs. kein
steps.body: To say "not" in German, you must choose between *nicht* and *kein*. Use *kein* to negate nouns, such as when you would say "no" or "not a" in English. Use *nicht* to negate verbs, adjectives, or adverbs. Think of *kein* as meaning "zero" of a thing.

steps.explain: "Zeit" is a noun, so we use "kein." Because "Zeit" is feminine, it becomes "keine."
"gut" is an adjective, so we use "nicht."
"Fußball" is a noun, so we use "kein."
